questions.prompt: Explain which view grows and which shrinks in a title-and-badge row. How do hugging and compression priorities express different decisions?
questions.scenario: A synthetic row needs a 180-point title, a 60-point badge, and 12 points of spacing. Its parent supplies either 300 or 220 points.
questions.androidBridge: ConstraintLayout and Compose measurement help frame size negotiation, but Swift intrinsic-size priorities are optional inequalities, not Kotlin layout weights or Compose hard constraints. Raising hugging does not raise compression resistance.
rubric: States that hugging resists growth and compression resistance resists shrinkage.
Calculates 48 points of surplus and 32 points of shortage.
Assigns separate horizontal priorities according to the desired product behavior.
Explains how known width and multiline wrapping affect height.
Identifies required-constraint conflicts and a minimum-width fallback.
questions.answerHTML:
Intrinsic content size describes a view's preferred size. Horizontal hugging roughly prefers actual width no greater than intrinsic width; compression resistance prefers width no smaller. These are independent preferences. At 300 points, the row has 48 surplus points. Giving the title lower hugging lets it absorb that surplus while the badge stays compact. At 220 points, the row starts with a 32-point shortage. Giving the title lower compression resistance makes it the initial narrowing participant.

A multiline title can convert narrower width into additional height, provided its width is determined and vertical constraints allow growth. The arithmetic predicts negotiation, not real font measurements. Inspect the actual instance priorities rather than assuming every control uses identical defaults. Required priority is 1000; making all competing preferences required can produce unsatisfiable constraints. If the badge and minimum readable title cannot fit, change to a vertical arrangement or another declared overflow policy. Verify narrow width, long localized text, and accessibility text sizes before accepting the row.
followUps: What changes if the title has no determined width or permits only one line?
How would you verify the intended winner without relying on equal competing priorities?
pitfalls: Treating higher hugging as protection against truncation.
Reporting synthetic width arithmetic as a device measurement.

questions.prompt: Diagnose a hosted scrolling form whose bottom gap doubles and whose focused field remains obscured. Which layout owner and guides would you inspect?
questions.scenario: A UIKit controller adds safe-area insets, its scroll wrapper adjusts content insets, and a SwiftUI child also avoids the keyboard.
questions.androidBridge: Kotlin Compose WindowInsets consumption suggests tracing inset ownership. UIKit safe areas, scroll adjustment, and keyboardLayoutGuide have distinct contracts; they do not follow Compose inset-consumption rules or automatically describe a floating keyboard.
rubric: Traces insets through controller, scroll wrapper, and hosted child.
Distinguishes safe area, readable width, keyboard, and scroll content guides.
Chooses one keyboard-avoidance owner and preserves reachable content.
Checks hosting containment and the component-specific sizing contract.
Plans narrow-width, large-text, and floating-keyboard observations.
questions.answerHTML:
Start by mapping every contributor to the bottom space: controller constraints, automatic scroll adjustment, explicit content insets, and the hosted child's safe-area or keyboard behavior. Safe areas describe obscuring system and container UI; they are not a complete keyboard-overlap model. Readable-width and margin guides serve different horizontal purposes. Removing all safe-area participation would hide the cause and can put interactive content under system UI.

Choose one keyboard-avoidance owner. UIKit's keyboardLayoutGuide can express keyboard relationships, while a scrolling form may instead manage keyboard-aware insets and scroll the active field into view. Floating keyboards require a deliberate policy. Constrain scroll content to its content guide and viewport width appropriately so large text can grow vertically. Check child-controller containment, hosting sizing, and the specific component's safe-area contract together; a local bridge convention is not universal guidance. Verify focus, dismissal, resizing, and accessibility text in a running scratch target. A corrected inset calculation alone does not prove the field is reachable or editing state survives.
followUps: How would you distinguish a doubled inset from an incorrect scroll-content height?
What additional behavior must you verify for an undocked iPad keyboard?
pitfalls: Ignoring every safe area to eliminate the visible gap.
Assuming keyboard avoidance supplies focus or a number-pad Done action.

questions.prompt: Why can a diffable list keep the right rows yet show an outdated subtitle? Explain identity, content updates, and complete cell configuration.
questions.scenario: The snapshot remains [A, B], but the content lookup for A changes. Later, C is inserted and the order becomes [C, B, A].
questions.androidBridge: Kotlin/Java RecyclerView stable IDs and DiffUtil suggest separating item identity from displayed content. UIKit snapshots use Hashable identifiers and explicit reconfiguration; RecyclerView payload and onBindViewHolder behavior is not an exact counterpart.
rubric: Separates immutable domain IDs, positions, cell instances, and reuse identifiers.
Keeps mutable subtitle data out of snapshot identity.
Explicitly reconfigures surviving changed IDs after updating the lookup.
Explains that reconfiguration does not require prepareForReuse.
Routes selection by current domain ID after insertion and reorder.
questions.answerHTML:
A diffable snapshot describes section and item identity plus order. An unchanged identifier does not necessarily cause UIKit to configure its cell again when an external content dictionary changes. Keep A as an immutable identifier, update its content in the lookup, and explicitly mark surviving changed IDs for reconfiguration. A newly inserted C receives initial configuration; it is not a surviving item. Identifiers must be unique across the snapshot.

Do not synthesize identity from the entire mutable display model: changing a subtitle could then look like replacing the item. Reconfiguration preserves an existing cell and does not call prepareForReuse for that update, so configuration must set every relevant visual and accessibility property. Reserve reload behavior for changes such as needing a different cell kind. Apply the content revision and snapshot through a serialized UI owner. Selection should resolve or capture A's domain ID rather than offset zero, which becomes C after insertion. Test subtitle changes, reorder, duplicate IDs, and delayed image completion separately.
followUps: When would reloading an item be more appropriate than reconfiguring it?
How would you prevent an old image completion from decorating a reused cell?
pitfalls: Hashing mutable presentation fields as permanent item identity.
Expecting prepareForReuse to clear every reconfiguration.

questions.prompt: Diagnose duplicate page loads and an old query error replacing newer results. How should pagination differ from thumbnail prefetch ownership?
questions.scenario: Repeated end-of-list callbacks start cursor p1 twice. Query B succeeds before query A fails, and canceling prefetch also cancels a visible row's shared image.
questions.androidBridge: Kotlin coroutine jobs and RecyclerView prefetch offer ownership analogies. Swift actor isolation does not make response order equal page order, and UIKit prefetch cancellation expresses predicted interest rather than ownership of every shared request.
rubric: Guards each in-flight cursor within a query generation.
Rejects obsolete success and failure outcomes.
Clears only the matching request's in-flight marker.
Keeps visible loading functional without prefetch.
Separates shared resource cancellation from an individual consumer's interest.
questions.answerHTML:
Give the page owner a query generation, next cursor, matching in-flight cursor, ordered IDs, and end state. Repeated threshold callbacks should start work only when that generation and cursor have no active request. Capture both before suspension. On success or failure, verify they still belong to the current query before changing rows, error state, or the in-flight marker. An old completion must not unlock a newer request. Serialize cursor-based loads or define explicit buffering if pages may finish out of order.

Preserve useful rows on a later-page failure and retry the failed cursor under the same guard. Define duplicate-ID merging and repeated-cursor behavior. Prefetch is a separate resource-interest mechanism: translate callback positions to current IDs, and ensure visible configuration can load missing content without any prefetch callback. Canceling one speculative interest should not cancel a shared image still needed by a visible consumer. Use controlled start signals and completion gates to release B before A, then exercise A's success and error paths.
followUps: What policy handles an empty page that still returns a next cursor?
Which assertions would distinguish duplicate-load prevention from stale-result rejection?
pitfalls: Guarding only successful responses with the query generation.
Making prefetch the only path that loads required content.

questions.prompt: Explain SwiftUI's proposal, response, and placement contract. What should a custom column do with unspecified, zero, and finite widths?
questions.scenario: A column measures multiline Text in a narrow parent and a vertical ScrollView. Its implementation currently replaces every nil proposal with zero.
questions.androidBridge: Compose measure and placement provide a useful sequence, but ProposedViewSize is a proposal rather than Compose Constraints. A nil Swift dimension asks for ideal behavior; it is not Kotlin null meaning an absent child.
rubric: Separates parent proposal, child-reported size, and final placement.
Distinguishes unspecified, zero, and unbounded probes.
Explains width-dependent multiline height.
Uses consistent measurement and placement policies with bounds origin.
Keeps sizing free of requests and observable-state mutation.
questions.answerHTML:
The parent proposes dimensions, each child chooses a size, and the parent places the resulting children. A child need not accept an exact proposed size, and the parent can probe several times. An unspecified dimension asks about ideal size; zero asks about minimum behavior; infinity probes maximum behavior. Replacing nil with zero changes the question and can collapse content. A concrete reported size still needs a meaningful finite result.

For a finite column width, measure text with that width and sum the returned heights plus spacing between children. Place using a consistent width policy and the final bounds origin. A narrower multiline Text may become taller, so cached measurements must remain valid for the actual inputs. Empty children should not create a phantom gap. A vertical ScrollView commonly leaves the scrolling dimension unspecified rather than imposing viewport height. Define overflow behavior for children that exceed the budget. Layout methods can run repeatedly, so they are unsuitable lifecycle hooks for networking or state mutation. Verify different probes and final rendering separately.
followUps: How could a GeometryReader used as the main child alter the size being measured?
Which inputs would invalidate a cached multiline measurement?
pitfalls: Treating every proposed dimension as a hard size constraint.
Returning infinity as the layout's concrete reported height.

questions.prompt: Diagnose a scroll control that flickers after adding a second geometry reporter. How do preference reduction, coordinate spaces, and feedback affect correctness?
questions.scenario: A bottom-marker PreferenceKey overwrites contributions. A second child now reports geometry, and showing the scroll control changes the measured content.
questions.androidBridge: Compose onGloballyPositioned offers a geometry-observation analogy, but SwiftUI PreferenceKey reduces descendant contributions upward. Kotlin callback order and Compose coordinates do not define SwiftUI reduction or layout-feedback semantics.
rubric: Identifies the original single-contributor assumption.
Selects a deliberate reduction rule for multiple contributors.
Compares positions in the same named coordinate space.
Explains the geometry-state-layout feedback cycle.
Plans no-op guards and stable control geometry.
questions.answerHTML:
The original overwrite reducer had a single bottom-marker contract. Adding another emitter changes its meaning: the last contribution is not automatically the bottom or the maximum. First decide what the ancestor needs. Use one dedicated marker, a maximum with compatible semantics, or an ID-keyed collection with an explicit merge rule. Do not choose a reducer merely because it removes flicker.

Measure positions in the intended named scroll coordinate space. A global position and local viewport height are not comparable just because both are numbers. Put an observing GeometryReader in a background or overlay when it should inspect existing assigned geometry rather than become the main sizing child. Then trace the loop: a preference updates state, state shows a control, the control changes geometry, and a new preference reverses the decision. Ignore unchanged values and keep the control's geometry from destabilizing its own threshold. Test keyboard, safe-area, content, and window changes. Prefer direct layout calculation when the value serves only layout rather than interaction.
followUps: When is taking the maximum a valid reducer, and when would it lose identity?
How would you distinguish a coordinate-space error from a feedback loop?
pitfalls: Assuming overwrite reduction remains valid with several emitters.
Mirroring every child frame into observable model state.

questions.prompt: Explain what withAnimation changes and how it differs from a transition. How should repeated taps and reduced motion affect a disclosure's final state?
questions.scenario: A disclosure inserts details when expanded. A broad animation modifier also animates validation errors, and code waits for the animation duration before committing selection.
questions.androidBridge: Compose animate-as-state suggests interpolation toward state, but SwiftUI transactions and insertion transitions have their own scope. Neither a Kotlin delay nor an animation duration is a correctness boundary for delivering a result.
rubric: Makes semantic state authoritative before visual completion.
Distinguishes animating an existing value from insertion or removal.
Explains transaction scope and simultaneous unrelated changes.
Preserves final meaning under interrupted animation.
Treats reduced motion as a visual policy rather than a disabled action.
questions.answerHTML:
withAnimation attaches animation information to a synchronous state mutation. The Boolean changes immediately; eligible visual differences interpolate toward that destination. It does not delay business state, make every property animatable, or keep unrelated async work alive. A transition describes a child entering or leaving the hierarchy. Applying an opacity transition to a permanently present child does not create insertion.

Keep disclosure visibility derived from the latest Boolean, so repeated taps can interrupt interpolation without leaving a contradictory final hierarchy. A value-watching animation modifier can affect other simultaneous changes inside its scope. Narrow that scope if an unrelated error or keyboard adjustment should update directly. Selection delivery needs its own ownership and exactly-once policy; waiting for a nominal duration cannot establish completion or freshness. Reduced motion should change or remove the visual interpolation while preserving the action and final state. Verify rapid toggling, interrupted navigation, and reduced-motion completion in a running target. A static screenshot demonstrates appearance at one instant, not interruption behavior.
followUps: What state can be lost if the implementation replaces identity to trigger an effect?
How would you test semantic completion without depending on animation timing?
pitfalls: Using animation duration as synchronization for selection delivery.
Assuming a transition animates any permanently present property.

questions.prompt: Diagnose a draggable row that jumps, steals scrolling, and loses keyboard focus after reordering. Define the state and identity boundaries before adjusting gestures.
questions.scenario: Every onChanged adds the full drag translation to a saved offset. Scroll callbacks retain an old proxy, and two text fields share the same focus case.
questions.androidBridge: Compose pointer input and focus requesters suggest transient interaction owners. SwiftUI GestureState reset, gesture precedence, ScrollViewReader proxy scope, and FocusState cases are distinct contracts rather than exact Kotlin API equivalents.
rubric: Renders committed offset plus current translation without repeated accumulation.
Commits once and defines cancellation and movement bounds.
Investigates recognizer competition and provides a semantic alternative.
Uses stable current scroll IDs and the current reader proxy.
Assigns unique focus cases without reconstructing the draft.
questions.answerHTML:
Drag translation is relative to the gesture's start. Adding the whole translation on every update double-counts movement. Keep committed offset in persistent state and current translation in GestureState. Render their sum, clamp the candidate to the allowed container if required, and commit the bounded result once on successful ending. GestureState resets on cancellation; do not convert a canceled transient displacement into a second commit.

A row drag competes with scrolling and navigation recognizers. Define the target region, direction, and minimum distance before choosing simultaneous or higher-priority composition. Those modifiers cannot certify correct arbitration. Provide buttons or accessibility actions for essential operations. After reorder, scroll to a stable domain ID through the proxy inside the current ScrollViewReader context rather than a retained appearance-time closure. Give each field a distinct optional focus case and clear focus explicitly on dismissal. Resizing or keyboard dismissal should preserve the draft owner. Verify cancellation, actual scrolling, focus progression, and alternative input; directly invoking callbacks tests logic but not recognizers.
followUps: Which geometry should bound movement when the scene resizes?
How would you prove reordering preserves the intended scroll target and field identity?
pitfalls: Accumulating start-relative translation repeatedly.
Applying highPriorityGesture as a universal fix for scrolling conflicts.

questions.prompt: Write the safe replacement step for a UITextFieldDelegate edit, then explain its units and its limitations during text composition.
questions.scenario: The current text is A🙂B. The text system supplies NSRange(location: 1, length: 2) and replacement X; paste and deletion must use the same path.
questions.androidBridge: Java and Kotlin String indexing also exposes UTF-16 units. Swift String.Index is not an integer offset, and its Character iteration follows grapheme clusters; neither Java char arithmetic nor String.count can replace range conversion.
rubric: Converts the supplied NSRange against the exact current string.
Handles failed conversion without force-unwrapping.
Replaces the entire supplied range with the entire replacement.
Predicts AXB and distinguishes UTF-16 units from Character count.
Preserves marked text and acknowledges separate grapheme-boundary validation.
questions.answerHTML:
Use Foundation's conversion against the same buffer that received the edit:

guard let edit = Range(range, in: current) else {
    return nil
}
return current.replacingCharacters(in: edit, with: replacement)

The helper returns an optional String so an invalid range has an explicit failure path. UIKit's range is in UTF-16 units. In A🙂B, the emoji occupies two such units, so location 1 and length 2 replace it with X and produce AXB. The replacement may contain several characters or be empty for deletion; do not process only its first character.

Swift Character count, UTF-8 byte count, and UTF-16 length are different units. Successful conversion alone does not certify a fabricated range aligns to whole grapheme clusters; validate that separately if the domain requires it. While markedTextRange exists, aggressive rewriting or truncation can break input-method composition and selection. Prefer a raw editing buffer and a declared commit-time validation policy. Test actual paste, selected replacement, caret behavior, and composition in UIKit; the string helper proves only the transformation boundary.
followUps: What would change if the replacement were empty or contained several grapheme clusters?
Why does a pure replacement test not prove marked-text or caret behavior?
pitfalls: Treating NSRange.location as a Swift Character offset.
Assuming every partial-surrogate or partial-grapheme range must fail conversion.

questions.prompt: Diagnose a code form that loses a leading zero, rejects composition mid-edit, and shows an obsolete validation error. Separate input assistance from product rules.
questions.scenario: A five-ASCII-digit demo code is converted to Int on each keystroke. The number pad has no Return key, and an older server validation finishes after the text changes.
questions.androidBridge: Kotlin raw text state, InputType, and coroutine revision checks are useful analogies. UIKit keyboardType does not validate input, submitLabel cannot add a missing number-pad Return key, and Swift string units require an explicit rule.
rubric: Keeps the code as raw String data with its leading zero.
Names the ASCII-only submission contract and permits provisional editing.
Separates keyboard traits from paste and validation behavior.
Rejects obsolete validation success and failure by input revision.
Provides explicit dismissal and field-specific repairable errors.
questions.answerHTML:
Keep the editing code as a String. Integer conversion discards the leading zero and imposes numeric meaning on an identifier. For this synthetic rule, submission accepts exactly five ASCII digits; that is narrower than accepting all Unicode decimal digits. Permit provisional raw input and evaluate eligibility at a declared boundary instead of rewriting every intermediate buffer. Normalize only what the domain allows.

The number-pad keyboard assists entry but cannot prevent paste or prove validity. submitLabel changes an available action label; it does not create a Return key on a number pad. Supply an explicit Done action and a hardware-keyboard submit path, clearing focus without clearing buffers. Tag async validation with the input revision and check it before publishing either success or failure. Preserve the draft on server rejection and explain the field needing repair. Localize persistent labels and error text, allowing expansion at large text sizes. Pure rule tests cover leading zeros and invalid characters; actual keyboard, marked-text, selection, and scrolling interactions require separate runtime observations.
followUps: How would the acceptance tests change if the domain allowed non-ASCII decimal digits?
When should an error first appear, and how should invalid submission move focus?
pitfalls: Using the keyboard type as the only validator.
Publishing an old error because only successful validation checks freshness.

questions.prompt: Assign owners for account services, navigation, focus, and draft data in a two-window iPad feature. What does resizing or scene disconnection imply?
questions.scenario: Window A edits draft alpha while window B browses beta. A singleton stores both selection and presenter, and developers assume rotation recreates the screen.
questions.androidBridge: Kotlin/Java Activity and Android task lifetimes help discuss independent surfaces, but an iOS scene is not one Activity. Resizing does not imply Android configuration recreation, and a scene identifier is not a domain draft ID.
rubric: Separates process, scene, window, controller, and domain lifetimes.
Keeps navigation, presentation, and focus local to the initiating scene.
Declares whether drafts are shared or independently edited.
Distinguishes scene disconnection from permanent session or process destruction.
Routes logout invalidation across affected scenes and late work.
questions.answerHTML:
The process can own an authenticated service and account-scoped repository. Each scene root should own its navigation path, modal presentation, selected record, and focus requests. A window presents that scene's hierarchy; a controller owns a screen or container. Draft lifetime follows the product's editing and persistence contract, which may outlive a controller. If both windows edit the same document, explicitly choose live sharing, independent tentative buffers, or conflict resolution.

Route presentation through the scene or controller receiving the action. Selecting an arbitrary connected scene or global key window can present login in the wrong surface. Resizing changes available geometry; it does not inherently recreate an Android-style configuration instance or justify replacing the model. Scene disconnection can release scene-owned subscriptions and tasks without deleting a durable draft, and the session may reconnect later. Conversely, in-memory state cannot survive process death by itself. Logout must invalidate account-bound presentation, restoration, caches, and old async results in every relevant scene. A declared iPad destination is not evidence that these two-window semantics work.
followUps: How would independent tentative buffers reconcile commits to the same draft?
Which state should survive scene disconnection but not an account transition?
pitfalls: Using the first connected scene as the universal presenter.
Equating window resize with automatic controller and draft recreation.

questions.prompt: Design adoption of scene restoration for a draft feature. Assign ownership, compare storage alternatives, and define evidence, staged rollout, and recovery.
questions.scenario: The current feature restores a selected ID globally. A deleted record, account switch, or second window can replay an invalid destination after launch.
questions.androidBridge: Kotlin SavedStateHandle values and Room-backed drafts suggest separating presentation restoration from data persistence. SceneStorage and AppStorage have different scene versus defaults scopes; neither reproduces Android process-restoration semantics or grants access to a restored record.
rubric: Assigns scene restoration, durable storage, and account invalidation owners.
Compares lightweight scene state with repository-backed drafts.
Uses a versioned non-sensitive envelope and validates current records.
Defines two-window and process-restart evidence with explicit failure cases.
Stages adoption and provides fallback without replaying side effects.
questions.answerHTML:
Let the scene owner persist minimal presentation meaning: envelope version, account-scope marker, draft ID, and optional selected record. The repository owner protects durable draft data, while the account owner invalidates old envelopes and late work. Compare lightweight SceneStorage for selection with repository-backed drafts; AppStorage's shared defaults key can unintentionally couple windows. None of these wrappers alone supplies a sensitive document persistence model.

Restore dependencies normally, validate the envelope version and current account, load the draft, and resolve the selection against current data. Unknown versions, corrupt state, deleted records, or account mismatch fall back to a valid root. Do not restore credentials, stale proxies, or automatic submission. Require independent-window, resize, logout-during-load, and process-restart fixtures, measuring successful restoration and safe fallback by cause. Stage adoption for one bounded feature after its actual scene configuration is verified. Keep a recovery path that ignores incompatible envelopes and opens the list while preserving durable drafts. Disabling restoration should not delete user data or imply a completed app-wide scene migration.
followUps: How would the rollout distinguish an invalid envelope from a failed durable draft load?
What must be revalidated before an encoded navigation destination becomes visible?
pitfalls: Treating decoded navigation state as authorization or permission to resubmit.
Deleting durable drafts when disabling a presentation-restoration feature.

questions.prompt: Design the source-of-truth and sizing boundaries for a SwiftUI editor, reusable picker, and UIKit review summary. How do Cancel and reorder preserve meaning?
questions.scenario: A scratch draft owns name, code, and provider A. Review copies these values into new local state; the picker mutates selection while merely highlighting rows.
questions.androidBridge: Kotlin Compose state hoisting and AndroidView updates suggest a shared editing owner and an adapter. SwiftUI State preserves a locally owned observable instance, and UIViewRepresentable has distinct creation, update, and proposal-based sizing contracts.
rubric: Keeps raw buffers and committed selection in one scene-owned draft.
Separates tentative highlight from committed selection when Apply is required.
Resolves reordered providers by stable ID.
Updates the UIKit summary from current shared input.
Explains finite-width fitting and distinguishes view from controller containment.
questions.answerHTML:
The scene root owns the draft and navigation. The draft owns raw name and code buffers, committed provider ID, and current provider content. Review reads that same model rather than seeding new local State copies that drift. With Observation, a locally created observable reference can be held in root State; an editor needing projected bindings uses the appropriate binding boundary.

A picker that commits immediately should mutate only on deliberate selection. An Apply-style picker instead owns a tentative highlight and copies it on confirmation; Cancel leaves the prior committed ID untouched. Resolve IDs against current content after insertion or reorder, and block Review if the selected provider disappears. The UIKit representable creates a label once, updates its text from current input, and fits multiline content against finite proposed width. Larger text or narrower width may increase height; unspecified sizing can defer to the bridge's default strategy. A UILabel needs no child-controller containment, whereas a hosted controller does. Verify reorder, cancellation, wrapping, focus dismissal, and shared model identity as separate contracts.
followUps: How should Review respond when its selected provider is removed?
Which evidence proves the label wraps rather than merely compiling its sizeThatFits method?
pitfalls: Creating independent review state from an initial draft snapshot.
Committing tentative picker changes during cancellation.

questions.prompt: Propose an acceptance and adoption plan for the integrated UI flow. Compare evidence layers, assign owners, and define rollout gates and recovery for invalid selection or stale work.
questions.scenario: A synthetic demo looks correct once, but paging, IME composition, large text, restoration, and two-window behavior remain unverified.
questions.androidBridge: Kotlin/Java unit tests, Android screenshots, and instrumentation tests motivate layered evidence. A Swift logic fake cannot certify UIKit recognizer or IME behavior, and an iOS simulator snapshot does not establish independent-window or physical-device performance.
rubric: Maps sizing, editing, identity, and scene risks to distinct owners.
Chooses focused logic, rendering, and interaction evidence.
Uses explicit start/completion gates for stale success and failure.
Defines bounded staged adoption and correctness gates.
Provides recoverable selection and restoration outcomes with honest coverage limits.
questions.answerHTML:
Assign the draft owner validation and committed selection, the page owner query freshness, the bridge owner sizing updates, and the scene owner navigation and restoration. Compare pure tests for format and generation rules with snapshots for long text and actual interactions for keyboard, cancellation, and window behavior. A single end-to-end script is broader but less precise at locating each failure.

Use explicit fake start signals, complete B before A, then release both old success and old failure. Assert current rows, error state, selection, and matching in-flight markers. Add reorder-safe selection and Cancel fixtures. Measure the UIKit summary at declared widths and text categories, and observe composition and focused-field reachability in a running target. Stage adoption behind a bounded feature boundary only after applicable gates pass; record unexecuted device or two-window rows as pending. If a selection vanishes or restoration fails, preserve editable buffers and offer a valid root or renewed choice. Retain a known-good flow for recovery, without erasing drafts or treating the teaching reference as completed production work.
followUps: Which minimal fixture would expose an old completion incorrectly clearing a newer in-flight marker?
How would you decide whether a rendering difference blocks adoption or needs a baseline review?
pitfalls: Claiming one screenshot proves editing, restoration, and asynchronous ownership.
Re-recording baselines to conceal an unexplained regression.

questions.prompt: Define a trustworthy search-to-usable-results measurement and its signposts. How does a mapping interval differ from the full operation?
questions.scenario: A synthetic search awaits data, maps rows, and presents results. Its current timer ends immediately after constructing a Task.
questions.androidBridge: Android trace sections and coroutine timing suggest operation boundaries. Swift signpost interval identity and lifetime still need explicit pairing; constructing a Task, like launching a Kotlin coroutine, does not measure its awaited work.
rubric: Defines start, usable endpoint, fixture, and outcome denominator.
Keeps mapping as a nested diagnostic interval.
Pairs overlapping interval identities through success, failure, and cancellation.
Separates elapsed time, CPU work, and presented responsiveness.
Records environment and bounded non-sensitive metadata.
questions.answerHTML:
Define the operation before selecting the tool. Start at an accepted synthetic search action and end when the correct results are presented and the declared interaction is usable. Specify fixture, cache state, device, OS, build configuration, and failure classification. A timer ending after Task construction measures scheduling rather than the task's awaited outcome. Await the relevant work and pair the interval through successful completion, thrown failure, and cancellation.

Keep a separate mapping interval inside the larger operation to test a CPU-transformation hypothesis. Give overlapping operations distinct interval identities while retaining bounded names. Elapsed time includes waiting; Time Profiler can investigate CPU stacks; rendering evidence establishes presentation and responsiveness. These answer different questions. Retain raw observations and failed or canceled outcomes according to the declared denominator, rather than silently dropping them. Metadata should identify bounded phases and fixtures without logging raw queries or account data. A source signpost establishes instrumentation intent only; actual traces and minimally instrumented confirmation runs are still required for a performance claim.
followUps: How would cancellation count in the denominator for latency and wasted-work reports?
Which tool would distinguish queue wait from synchronous mapping CPU cost?
pitfalls: Timing task creation and calling it completed search latency.
Treating a mapping microbenchmark as proof of usable-screen improvement.

questions.prompt: Review a performance report that averages device p95 values and adds phase p95 values. What can its samples actually support?
questions.scenario: One cohort has five samples; another has twenty. The report calls nearest-rank p50 the conventional median and deletes failed runs.
questions.androidBridge: Kotlin benchmark libraries may expose percentile summaries, but a library result does not define the experiment's denominator. Swift array indexing and nearest-rank arithmetic differ only syntactically; cohort and statistical limits remain essential.
rubric: Calculates nearest-rank selection using ceil(p times n) minus one.
Explains that five-sample p95 is the maximum.
Distinguishes nearest-rank p50 from an even-sample conventional median.
Rejects averaging cohort p95 or summing unrelated phase p95.
Retains raw order, outcomes, conditions, and sample-size limits.
questions.answerHTML:
Nearest-rank p95 sorts n samples and selects one-based rank ceil(0.95 times n), then subtracts one for a Swift array index. For twenty ordered values from 1 through 20, it selects 19. For five samples, it selects the maximum. These are reproducible arithmetic results, not strong evidence about a population tail. Nearest-rank p50 selects the tenth of twenty values, while a conventional even-sample median averages the tenth and eleventh.

Keep device cohorts separate. Averaging their p95 values does not produce a fleet percentile; combining raw observations requires an explicit weighting and sampling model. Likewise, total-operation p95 is not generally the sum of phase p95 values, because different operations can be slow in different phases. Retain paired phase observations to attribute the actual tail. Restore failed, canceled, and invalid-preparation records with declared classifications. Report raw samples, count, range, units, estimator, and thermal/cache conditions. More decimal places do not repair a small, drifting, or selectively filtered experiment.
followUps: How would paired per-operation phases help explain the slowest observed searches?
What preparation rule could justify rerunning a sample without silently deleting it?
pitfalls: Calling the average of two p95 values the fleet p95.
Removing slow failures after seeing the result.

questions.prompt: Explain the launch critical path and why delegate completion, first frame, and first usable interaction are different endpoints.
questions.scenario: A synthetic app assigns its root quickly, but account reconciliation and store migration continue behind a spinner before a deep link can open.
questions.androidBridge: Kotlin/Java Android startup initializers suggest a dependency graph, but iOS process preparation, delegate or scene callbacks, and presentation metrics have different contracts. Completing a callback is not equivalent to Android fully drawn or usable content.
rubric: Includes runtime preparation before familiar app callbacks.
Draws routing dependencies on account and migration readiness.
Defines first frame and usable content separately.
Identifies the longest required chain rather than summing concurrent work.
Declares terminated-process and resume preparation conditions.
questions.answerHTML:
Launch begins before the app delegate: code loading, runtime preparation, and initializers can contribute. App setup then creates the root, performs layout, commits a frame, and eventually presents it. That frame may still be a loading screen. Define usable content separately: required initialization is complete, the permitted route is visible, and a meaningful first interaction succeeds. Root assignment or viewDidAppear alone cannot certify all of those conditions.

Draw dependencies explicitly. A consumer needing migrated data waits for migration; an authenticated route waits for account reconciliation. The critical path is the longest necessary dependency chain, not the sum of every concurrent phase. Extra parallel work can add contention without shortening it. Specify preparation for terminated-process launches, returning-account launches, deep links, and process-surviving resume; do not call every case cold. Record uncertain OS cache state. Use supported launch measurements for first-frame evidence and a defined readiness boundary for usability, then verify the first tap. Source tracing identifies candidate phases, but supplies no timing or completed launch measurement.
followUps: How would you classify telemetry that must start early enough to observe launch?
Why can a faster first frame still make the first interaction worse?
pitfalls: Ending the launch experiment at root-controller assignment.
Summing all concurrent startup spans as the critical path.

questions.prompt: Design a bounded startup optimization proposal. Compare deferral and dependency or resource reduction, assign owners, and define measurement, rollout, and recovery.
questions.scenario: A team proposes lazily initializing several SDKs and changing framework linkage to improve launch and reduce size, without a matched baseline.
questions.androidBridge: Kotlin lazy initialization and Android APK size analysis suggest tradeoffs. Swift Task creation can inherit MainActor isolation, and static or dynamic iOS linkage has different packaging costs; no fixed per-framework saving follows from the analogy.
rubric: Assigns dependency, feature-readiness, and release-artifact ownership.
Compares alternatives against a measured critical phase.
Preserves account, migration, and instrumentation ordering.
Separates launch, first-interaction, download, and installed-size evidence.
Stages one change with corrective-build and behavior-recovery criteria.
questions.answerHTML:
First obtain matched launch and exported-artifact baselines, then select one measured bottleneck. Assign the startup owner dependency ordering, feature owners readiness and first-use behavior, and the release owner packaging verification. Compare deferring independent initialization with removing unused work or reducing a dependency/resource boundary. A linkage change deserves its own loader and packaging investigation; framework count does not imply a fixed timing penalty.

Classify work as required before presentation, required before usability, or opportunistic. Preserve account reconciliation, migration, and early instrumentation dependencies. Give deferred work a lifetime and failure policy; Task creation inside MainActor code does not automatically move synchronous initialization off the UI executor. Measure first frame, usable route, and first interaction under identical fixtures. Track executable, resources, download, and installed size as separate quantities. Stage one bounded candidate only after correctness and artifact checks. Define recovery as restoring prior initialization order or producing a verified corrective build for packaging changes. Record pending device observations rather than promising gains from the design.
followUps: What evidence would show lazy initialization merely moved the stall to the first tap?
Which rollback inputs are needed if the candidate also changes a binary dependency?
pitfalls: Assuming Task makes synchronous startup work background execution.
Using one file-size figure as download and installed-size evidence.

questions.prompt: Explain commit hitches, render hitches, and hangs. How would you choose evidence for a scrolling screen that misses presentation deadlines?
questions.scenario: One candidate trace shows main-thread row mapping near a missed commit; another shows expensive compositing after the app commits on time.
questions.androidBridge: Kotlin/Java Android View traversal and RenderThread offer a pipeline analogy. UIKit or SwiftUI commits through Core Animation and downstream rendering have distinct tracks; Android frame-stage names and budgets are not exact iOS counterparts.
rubric: Separates app commit work from downstream rendering and presentation.
Distinguishes continuous-motion hitches from discrete unresponsiveness.
Correlates selected missed deadlines with stacks and render tracks.
Avoids assigning the entire frame interval to each function.
Confirms a candidate under a matched minimally instrumented gesture.
questions.answerHTML:
A frame passes through event handling and UI updates, Core Animation commit, downstream rendering, and display presentation. A commit hitch occurs when app work misses its commit deadline. A render hitch can occur after a timely commit when rendering misses its own deadline. A hang describes a period of unresponsiveness, often around a discrete interaction; a hitch interrupts continuous motion. One blocking operation can contribute to either depending on timing.

For the mapping hypothesis, select a missed commit interval and inspect relevant main-thread stacks and signposts. For the compositing hypothesis, inspect the render portion after the timely commit rather than assuming more background CPU work will help. Refresh cadence supplies deadline context, not a complete allowance for each method. Average CPU can hide a short badly timed burst. Keep gesture, content, image-cache state, text size, and device conditions fixed. After diagnosis, confirm the candidate with lighter instrumentation and the same interaction. A smooth-looking simulator pass or a print count cannot establish physical-device frame behavior.
followUps: How could a background worker still contribute to a UI deadline miss?
What would you inspect if the commit improved but scrolling still hitches?
pitfalls: Diagnosing all scrolling problems from average CPU alone.
Giving every function an entire refresh interval as its budget.

questions.prompt: Diagnose a SwiftUI list that recomputes sorting during progress updates and loses row state after insertion. What does body evaluation prove?
questions.scenario: A 500-row synthetic list reads progress in its parent, sorts in body, and identifies rows by offsets. A print statement is being used as a redraw counter.
questions.androidBridge: Kotlin Compose recomposition dependencies and stable keys suggest narrowing reads and preserving identity. SwiftUI Observation tracks accessed properties differently from ObservableObject publication, and body evaluation is not a direct Compose recomposition or displayed-frame count.
rubric: Moves unchanged projection work to the accepted data-revision boundary.
Narrows progress reads to a relevant leaf.
Uses stable domain IDs rather than offsets.
Separates evaluation, reconciliation, layout, commit, and presentation.
Verifies behavior before claiming measured hitch improvement.
questions.answerHTML:
The parent establishes a dependency by reading progress, so frequent updates can trigger evaluation that repeats sorting. Compute the unchanged row projection when a new data revision is accepted and expose the result. Move progress reads into a relevant leaf, checking helper calls and aggregate inputs that may still broaden dependencies. Splitting functions alone does not guarantee narrower updates. Observation tracks accessed observable properties, while ObservableObject publication can have broader effects.

Use stable domain IDs in ForEach. Offsets change after insertion and can attach local state or actions to the wrong row. Preserve the observable owner's lifetime rather than recreating it during body evaluation. A body print counts evaluations with added overhead; it does not count displayed frames. Evaluation, reconciliation, layout, layer commit, and presentation are separate work. Prove sorting semantics, insertion identity, titles, actions, and cancellation before timing. Correlate update duration with actual hitch intervals and confirm on a matched gesture. Do not claim the dependency cleanup eliminates image decode or render-server cost.
followUps: How could passing a frequently changing aggregate to every row preserve broad invalidation?
Which fixture would catch an equality shortcut that hides a changed action?
pitfalls: Using body prints as a presented-frame counter.
Replacing stable item identity with array offsets.

questions.prompt: Explain Swift Array value semantics and copy-on-write. Why can a small slice retain substantial memory, and what does copying class elements actually copy?
questions.scenario: A synthetic history keeps old array versions while mutating the newest. Another component retains a short ArraySlice after releasing the original binding.
questions.androidBridge: Assigning a Kotlin List usually shares a reference; the read-only interface does not promise an independent snapshot. Swift Array preserves value semantics with possible shared storage, but arrays of class instances still share the referenced objects.
rubric: Distinguishes logical value independence from immediate buffer copying.
Explains shared versus uniquely owned mutation.
Identifies retained old versions and slice backing storage.
Distinguishes element references from deep-copied objects.
Separates semantic assertions from allocation measurements and thread safety.
questions.answerHTML:
Assigning a Swift Array creates another logical value. Storage can initially be shared through copy-on-write, and mutating shared storage can require separation. A uniquely owned mutation can avoid that copy. Verify that the original value remains unchanged, but do not promise a particular allocation instruction: optimization and bridging affect implementation details. Retaining many old snapshots while editing the newest can keep several buffers alive.

An ArraySlice can retain a large backing allocation even when its visible range is small. Converting the needed range to a small Array trades immediate copying for potentially releasing that backing storage. Measure the actual allocation and retention under an equivalent optimized configuration. If elements are class instances, array storage contains references: copying or separating the array does not clone the objects, so mutating an element's properties can be visible through both arrays. Copy-on-write also does not make concurrent mutation of the same variable safe. Separate tests for value semantics, object ownership, transient copying cost, and retained memory population.
followUps: How would you keep both values observable in an optimized copy-on-write experiment?
When might copying a tiny slice be preferable despite its immediate work?
pitfalls: Assuming every assignment eagerly deep-copies array storage and objects.
Treating copy-on-write as synchronization for a shared mutable variable.

questions.prompt: Diagnose memory peaks in an 80-point thumbnail grid. Why are compressed bytes, view bounds, retained cache size, and concurrent decoding different budgets?
questions.scenario: Several 4000-by-3000 JPEGs decode concurrently on a scale-three display. The final cache is small, but the report assumes small UIImageView frames imply small decoded buffers.
questions.androidBridge: Android Bitmap decoding and thumbnail sampling offer a pixel-budget analogy. UIImageView bounds do not set ImageIO decode dimensions, and Objective-C autorelease lifetime differs from Kotlin garbage collection or coroutine suspension.
rubric: Calculates 48 million bytes for the stated four-byte pixel estimate.
Converts 80 points at scale three to a 240-pixel display requirement.
Explains downsampling before needless full-source materialization.
Bounds concurrent decodes and treats panorama or multi-frame policy separately.
Separates estimated pixels, transient peak, retained objects, and measured footprint.
questions.answerHTML:
A four-byte-per-pixel estimate for 4000 by 3000 pixels is 48 million bytes, about 45.8 MiB, before padding, intermediates, or other overhead. Compressed JPEG size does not describe that decoded budget. An 80-point destination on a scale-three display suggests roughly 240 pixels per side. Resizing the view or scaling an already decoded image does not ensure the source was decoded at that size.

Use a bounded ImageIO thumbnail path with orientation transformation, then verify output dimensions and quality. A longest-edge bound preserves aspect ratio; a panorama filling a square needs a separate crop or accepted-quality policy. Bound active decodes as well as retained cache cost, because several large intermediates can dominate the peak. Inspect allocations, footprint, and route-exit retention independently. A synchronous autorelease pool can shorten some Objective-C temporary lifetimes, but it should not enclose await or be expected to drain future callbacks. Compare equivalent source fixtures and appearance, and label pixel arithmetic as estimated until actual memory evidence exists.
followUps: How would you distinguish a decode peak from a retained screen-owner cycle?
Which additional limits would you declare for animated or untrusted image sources?
pitfalls: Using compressed file bytes as the decoded-cache budget.
Claiming small view bounds guarantee downsampled decoding.

questions.prompt: Outline a task-group loader with a positive concurrency window and ordered output. Which limits and cancellation checks does that algorithm establish?
questions.scenario: A batch has many synthetic inputs. The current version creates one task per input, waits for permits, then compactMaps incomplete output after cancellation.
questions.androidBridge: Kotlin coroutine workers or a semaphore suggest bounded execution. Swift task groups return completion order and join their children; a semaphore around thousands of created tasks, in either language, does not bound queued captures or payload bytes.
rubric: Seeds at most the positive limit and replenishes after completion.
Returns input indexes and lets the parent own output mutation.
Checks cancellation before replacement work and publication.
Preserves cancellation and failures instead of publishing incomplete success.
Distinguishes active-task, queue, payload-byte, and request-rate limits.
questions.answerHTML:
Reject a nonpositive limit and return an empty result for empty input. Seed the group with at most the limit's worth of inputs. Each child returns its input index and loaded immutable value. As the parent receives a completion, store it in that index's slot and add at most one replacement after checking cancellation. Only the parent mutates the output array, preserving input order even when completion order differs.

Let meaningful child failure escape under the declared policy so the structured scope cancels and joins remaining work. Children must cooperate; the group cannot force an unresponsive legacy call to stop. Check cancellation before admission and before publishing. Validate that every expected output exists rather than using compactMap to disguise missing work as success. This window bounds initially created and active children, but not final output size, each payload's bytes, or requests per second. Give those separate budgets. Use gated fakes to complete later inputs first and verify ordering, peak active calls, empty input, and cancellation without timing sleeps.
followUps: What happens to scope completion if a canceled fake never resumes?
How would you specify partial failure without silently changing the successful-output contract?
pitfalls: Calling a permit-limited queue of thousands of tasks bounded memory.
Using compactMap to turn cancellation into a shorter successful result.

questions.prompt: Design a shared loading service under memory and energy constraints. Compare loss policies and coalescing alternatives, assign owners, and define measurement, staged rollout, and recovery.
questions.scenario: Visible and prefetched rows share downloads. A callback stream outpaces decoding, logout occurs during transfer, and one departing waiter cancels everyone's work.
questions.androidBridge: Kotlin Flow suspension and shared coroutine ownership suggest demand and waiter policies. AsyncStream bufferingNewest drops buffered elements rather than suspending producers, and awaiting an unstructured Swift Task does not automatically propagate waiter cancellation.
rubric: Assigns shared-operation, waiter, cache-commit, and UI-publication ownership.
Compares replacement progress with lossless ordered-event handling.
Declares queue bytes, active work, priority, and rate budgets separately.
Validates account epoch at cache commit and feature generation at publication.
Defines device measurements, phased adoption, and bounded fallback.
questions.answerHTML:
Let the service own a coalesced operation and each consumer own its interest. Canceling one waiter should follow policy without abandoning other active waiters; define what happens when the last leaves. Compare coalescing with independent requests using transfer, latency, and memory evidence. Prioritize visible demand over speculative prefetch through a documented admission policy.

For streams, replaceable progress may use a newest-value buffer. Ordered tokens or commands need demand-aware delivery, a pull source, or explicit overflow failure and recovery. An element count is not a byte budget. Independently bound queued bytes, active transfers, decoding, and request rate. The cache owner checks account epoch in its commit domain, while the UI owner checks its query generation before publication. Stage one consumer after gated cancellation/logout fixtures and matched device comparisons of throughput, p95, peak memory, and supported energy observations. Under pressure, stop optional admission and recover gradually; avoid restart storms. Keep a known-good loading policy for rollback and never report battery savings from request-count reduction alone.
followUps: Which signals would distinguish beneficial coalescing from visible-demand priority inversion?
What recovery contract applies if a lossless stream exceeds its bounded byte budget?
pitfalls: Describing a dropping AsyncStream buffer as producer backpressure.
Checking account ownership only in the foreground caller before a later cache write.

questions.prompt: Sketch stable deduplication using a membership index. Explain order, equality, complexity, and memory before proposing it as a performance improvement.
questions.scenario: The input is [b, a, b, c]. A baseline repeatedly scans its output; a proposed replacement converts directly to Set and returns its elements.
questions.androidBridge: Kotlin LinkedHashSet suggests preserving first occurrence, but a plain Swift Set does not preserve the input-order contract. Swift String equality and hashing are not Java UTF-16 or byte-comparison semantics, so keep the declared identity policy.
rubric: Traverses input once and appends only newly inserted keys.
Predicts the full ordered output [b, a, c].
Explains quadratic scanning versus expected linear membership work.
Accounts for hashing, key projection, Unicode equality, and extra memory.
Requires semantic equivalence before matched optimized measurements.
questions.answerHTML:
Keep an output array and a Set of seen keys. Traverse the original input and append an element only when seen.insert(key).inserted is true. For [b, a, b, c], the result is [b, a, c]. The Set answers membership; the array preserves first-occurrence order. Returning arbitrary Set elements would change that observable contract.

Repeated contains checks on a growing array have quadratic worst-case membership comparisons for many distinct items. Indexed membership usually reduces that work to expected linear behavior over the input, with additional storage. Hashing and equality still cost time, particularly for long strings, and an expensive identity projection should be evaluated deliberately. Do not change case folding or normalization while claiming equivalence. Check complete outputs for empty, all-equal, all-distinct, mixed, and Unicode fixtures. Keep results observable under the same optimized configuration and construct fixtures outside a clearly named mapping-only interval. A microbenchmark can establish the mapping tradeoff; it does not independently establish screen responsiveness or energy gains.
followUps: How would a key projection change duplicate selection and its cost model?
Why might reserving excessive capacity hurt the memory tradeoff?
pitfalls: Returning an unordered Set while claiming stable first-occurrence output.
Calling theoretical expected complexity an observed device improvement.

questions.prompt: Review a claim that splitting a Swift module sped up both compilation and scrolling. What experiments distinguish build critical paths from runtime algorithms?
questions.scenario: A no-op build is compared with a clean build on another toolchain. A set-backed mapping is timed with fixture creation included only in the baseline.
questions.androidBridge: Gradle incremental-build and Kotlin algorithm analysis suggest separate investigations. Swift tools version, language mode, optimization, and generated module graph are independent inputs; faster type checking does not imply faster iOS execution.
rubric: Separates build-time and runtime hypotheses and reports.
Matches clean, no-op, and edit-triggered build preparation.
Inspects the build dependency critical path and earliest bottleneck.
Uses equivalent runtime boundaries and semantic assertions.
States module overhead and pending screen-level evidence.
questions.answerHTML:
The claim combines two different performance domains. For compilation, compare like preparation states: clean with clean, no-op with no-op, and a declared private or public edit with its equivalent. Keep host, compiler, destination, resolved graph, generated inputs, configuration, and cache policy fixed. Inspect the build timeline to locate type checking, dependency emission, linking, resources, or scripts. Module splitting can change rebuild scope and add graph overhead; its benefit is conditional.

For runtime mapping, first verify complete output equivalence, ordering, duplicate policy, and errors. Construct fixtures outside both mapping-only intervals or include them consistently in a broader named operation. Use the same optimized configuration, keep results observable, alternate matched runs, and retain raw samples. Expected algorithm growth predicts a candidate but is not measured speed. A faster build or mapping does not establish scrolling improvement. That needs a separate stable-identity gesture experiment and hitch evidence. Correct the report's mismatched denominators before attributing either result to the module change.
followUps: Why might a public API edit have a different incremental cost from a private implementation edit?
Which build evidence would justify a typed-expression rewrite before module splitting?
pitfalls: Comparing clean and warm builds as if their work were equivalent.
Including fixture construction in only one candidate's runtime interval.

questions.prompt: Design a controlled investigation for moving row projection out of repeated body evaluation. What must be proven before collecting and reporting timings?
questions.scenario: A synthetic candidate computes the same projection on accepted data revisions. Only a short profiler run exists, and an async timeout was recorded as a latency sample.
questions.androidBridge: Kotlin/Java Android benchmark and macrobenchmark harnesses suggest distinct boundaries. An XCTest timing harness, signposted iOS interaction, and physical-device trace each prove different contracts; a timeout is not completed latency in either ecosystem.
rubric: Freezes baseline, candidate, fixture, and falsifiable hypothesis.
Checks order, identity, empty/error states, and cancellation first.
Separates diagnostic tracing from matched confirmation samples.
Retains outcome classifications and paired phase observations.
Labels measured, source-derived, theoretical, and pending conclusions.
questions.answerHTML:
Freeze the two revisions, synthetic fixture, cache preparation, cohort, and hypothesis: moving an unchanged projection should reduce repeated synchronous work. Before timing, assert full ordering and equality, empty/error behavior, insertion identity, actions, and cancellation. A candidate that hides a changed action or stale result fails regardless of speed.

Use a diagnostic trace to correlate projection work with relevant commit or hitch intervals. Then collect matched, lighter-instrumentation operation samples under a declared warm-up and outcome policy, alternating or randomizing batches to reduce drift. Record raw order, units, sample count, estimator, cache and thermal conditions, failures, cancellation, and invalid preparation. An async timeout is an unfinished operation, not a successful latency sample. Keep paired phase data rather than adding unrelated phase p95 values. Add memory route cycles only when the change affects retention or peak. The handoff separates arithmetic and source reasoning from executed tests and device measurements, with reproducible commands and artifacts. Hardware-dependent results remain pending until actually collected.
followUps: What could heavier profiling change that requires a confirmation batch?
How would you make another engineer reproduce one cohort without guessing warm-up state?
pitfalls: Timing a candidate before checking equivalent observable behavior.
Counting an unfinished async timeout as a completed latency observation.

questions.prompt: Design ownership and adoption of performance regression gates. Compare absolute and paired budgets, define noise handling, and specify rollout and recovery decisions.
questions.scenario: A proposed gate uses an arbitrary p95 threshold and retries until green. Simulator measurements are being presented as phone smoothness and energy acceptance.
questions.androidBridge: Kotlin/Java Android performance CI suggests artifact retention and cohort budgets. Simulator XCTest baselines do not reproduce phone thermal, GPU, or energy behavior, just as host or emulator benchmarks cannot certify every Android device cohort.
rubric: Makes correctness the first hard gate.
Assigns fixture, budget, runner, and release decision owners.
Compares absolute user budgets with matched relative controls.
Uses observed variance and bounded rerun rules.
Stages gate enforcement and defines inspect, revert, or corrective-release outcomes.
questions.answerHTML:
Make correctness a hard gate before performance: stale or incomplete output never passes. Assign a fixture owner, runner owner, budget owner, and release decision role. Derive cohort-specific thresholds from baseline observations, variance, and product requirements. An absolute budget expresses user needs; a paired control helps expose runner drift. Compare both rather than inventing a threshold that merely accepts the current candidate.

Keep simulator CI and device release evidence separate. A simulator pass cannot certify phone rendering, memory pressure, or energy. Retain raw results, matching traces, failures, skips, and environmental changes so reviewers can distinguish regression from harness failure. Use a predeclared bounded rerun policy; repeated attempts until green hide instability. Stage new gates in observation mode, review noise and actionability, then enforce the validated boundaries. On failure, inspect or reproduce under the same protocol, revert the bounded candidate when regression is established, and use a corrective release if already distributed. Budget changes require an explained owner decision, not automatic relaxation.
followUps: What artifact would let a reviewer distinguish fixture preparation failure from a real regression?
When should a toolchain or fixture change require a new baseline rather than direct comparison?
pitfalls: Retrying without a bound until one run passes.
Treating a simulator gate as physical-device energy acceptance.

questions.prompt: Explain target, scheme action, configuration, destination, and runtime environment. Why does a scheme called Sandbox not prove the resulting app's identity or endpoint?
questions.scenario: A synthetic workspace can run a Debug production app or archive a Release sandbox app. Developers describe both choices as one flavor.
questions.androidBridge: Gradle product flavors and build types declared in Kotlin DSL form a variant graph, but an Xcode scheme is an action selection rather than one flavor. Swift compilation conditions, bundle identity, resources, and runtime endpoint are separate choices.
rubric: Defines each build axis and its responsibility.
Separates optimization configuration from service environment.
Explains scheme action-specific target and configuration selection.
Distinguishes declared settings from effective and built-artifact evidence.
Checks bundle identity and capabilities rather than trusting names.
questions.answerHTML:
A target defines a component and its output, such as an app, framework, extension, or test bundle. A scheme selects participants and settings for Run, Test, Archive, and other actions. A configuration provides build settings, while a destination chooses platform and runtime. Runtime service environment is another decision. Debug can use production services, and Release can use a sandbox if that contract is explicitly configured.

Scheme names describe intent, not the effective compiler conditions, installed bundle identifier, or endpoint. Follow the chosen action to its consuming target and configuration, then trace configuration includes, target overrides, resources, and the application's environment mapping. A user-defined build setting is not automatically readable by Swift code. Inspect bounded effective settings and compiler inputs, and verify the built bundle's identity and capabilities when artifact evidence is needed. Keep declaration, effective value, and observed behavior separate. Do not assume Xcode generates the same flavor cross-product as Gradle or that a directory named Sandbox participates in the selected action.
followUps: Why could Run and Archive under the same scheme select different configurations?
How would a build-setting environment value reach application code deliberately?
pitfalls: Equating a scheme name with a Gradle flavor and endpoint.
Assuming Release always means production services.

questions.prompt: Diagnose a sandbox build overwriting production while ignoring a new Swift condition. Which evidence resolves identity and setting-precedence failures?
questions.scenario: An xcconfig appends COURSE_SANDBOX with inheritance, but the target supplies its own condition list. Both installed artifacts unexpectedly use the same bundle identifier.
questions.androidBridge: Android applicationIdSuffix and Kotlin/Java BuildConfig access suggest separate installation and behavior inputs. Xcode bundle identifiers and SWIFT_ACTIVE_COMPILATION_CONDITIONS follow layered setting precedence; they are not automatically generated from Gradle flavor semantics.
rubric: Resolves the exact scheme action, target, configuration, and SDK.
Traces includes, inherited lists, conditions, and target overrides.
Inspects effective Swift conditions and the compiler invocation.
Checks the built bundle identifier and matching capability contract.
Separates flag-driven behavior from runtime endpoint configuration.
questions.answerHTML:
First identify the actual scheme action, consuming target, configuration, and SDK for each artifact. Trace the xcconfig include chain and subsequent assignments. Inherited expansion preserves lower-layer list values, but a higher-precedence target assignment can still replace the list. Inspect the effective compilation conditions and relevant compile invocation before concluding that the appended condition reaches Swift.

For installation overwrite, inspect the built bundle identifier rather than the scheme label. Trace its prefix expansion and target overrides, then review compatible signing and capability inputs without dumping sensitive settings. The identifier governs installation identity; changing a Swift condition alone does not create another app identity. Separately inspect how the runtime endpoint is selected, because compiler flags do not automatically configure a server. Compare bounded declared, effective, and artifact observations, and classify any Release-only import failure by target dependency and conditional membership. Avoid a broad cache reset until the graph and precedence evidence identify an actual stale artifact.
followUps: Could inherited expansion preserve an unwanted condition as well as a needed one?
What changes if the target edge exists in a generated graph but not a retained project?
pitfalls: Assuming an xcconfig append survives every target override.
Changing only a compilation flag to solve installation identity.

questions.prompt: Trace package, product, target module, requirement, and resolved revision. How do a version-looking branch and a framework filename mislead compatibility reasoning?
questions.scenario: The lesson's dependency audit includes a branch named 4.1.3 and a mocks product with different linkage declarations across graph routes.
questions.androidBridge: Gradle coordinates and dependency locks for Kotlin/Java modules suggest requirements versus selections. SwiftPM products expose target modules, and package resolution belongs to a consumer graph; Maven-style versions and AAR filenames do not define Swift linkage or module stability.
rubric: Separates package identity, product exposure, and importable target module.
Distinguishes requirement semantics from a selected revision.
Treats a version-looking branch as a branch.
Separates static or dynamic linking from framework packaging.
Distinguishes source, ABI, module, and runtime compatibility.
questions.answerHTML:
A package is a dependency unit with a manifest; a product exposes one or more targets for consumers; a target commonly defines an importable module. A requirement describes allowed selections, while the relevant consumer's Package.resolved records the selected revision and version or branch state. A branch named 4.1.3 remains a branch, not an exact semantic-version requirement. A dependency's own lockfile does not universally force downstream resolution.

Static and dynamic describe linking behavior, not just whether an artifact ends in framework. Different graph routes can declare different linkage, which deserves consumer review rather than an automatic bug claim. Source compatibility asks whether code compiles against the API. ABI describes compiled calling and layout contracts; module stability concerns compiler consumption of interfaces. Swift runtime ABI stability does not make arbitrary vendor binaries interchangeable. Check interfaces, platform variants, minimum OS, resources, and the consuming route. A resolved pin is neither proof of runtime execution nor a claim that the dependency is the latest available release.
followUps: Why must an arm64 device slice be distinguished from an arm64 simulator slice?
Which inputs would reproduce the selected graph after a bounded dependency change?
pitfalls: Reading a branch name that looks like a version as an exact release pin.
Inferring linkage and compatibility from a framework suffix alone.

questions.prompt: Design a review and adoption plan for a synthetic VendorCodec XCFramework. Compare source and binary alternatives, assign owners, and define compatibility evidence, rollout, and reconstruction.
questions.scenario: The vendor supplies only a device build and a compiler-specific swiftmodule. An initial import succeeds on one machine, and the team proposes immediate broad adoption.
questions.androidBridge: Kotlin/Java libraries packaged in Android AARs and native-library review suggest provenance and ABI coverage. XCFramework platform variants, swiftinterface module stability, and library evolution are separate Swift distribution contracts rather than JVM bytecode compatibility.
rubric: Assigns API, graph, packaging, provenance, and license review responsibilities.
Compares rebuilt source with independently distributed binaries.
Checks device/simulator variants, interfaces, dependencies, resources, and runtime floor.
Separates compile, link, load, and runtime availability evidence.
Stages one consumer and preserves prior artifact inputs for recovery.
questions.answerHTML:
Assign the contract owner API semantics, the graph owner dependency inputs, the platform owner destination and packaging checks, and appropriate reviewers provenance, licensing, and data behavior. Compare a source package rebuilt with the app against the vendor binary's distribution constraints. A successful local import is only one gate. Inspect distinct device and simulator variants, minimum OS, dependencies, resources, checksums, and interfaces.

A compiler-specific swiftmodule can limit consumption across compiler versions; textual interfaces and appropriate distribution support address a different boundary from stable runtime ABI. Classify import, duplicate-symbol, missing-framework, and unavailable-API failures separately. Verify supported consumers through compile, link, artifact inspection, and runtime checks, including extensions when affected. Stage one bounded consumer after its semantic and integration evidence passes. Retain the prior manifest, resolution, generator/compiler inputs, resource contents, and binary checksum for reconstruction. Define containment and a corrective-build path if the candidate is distributed. Do not call checksum verification license approval, or assume rebuilding prior source downgrades installed clients.
followUps: When is BUILD_LIBRARY_FOR_DISTRIBUTION useful, and why not enable it indiscriminately?
What additional evidence is required if the binary imports successfully but its resources are missing?
pitfalls: Treating one compiler import as complete distribution compatibility.
Assuming equal CPU architecture makes device and simulator variants interchangeable.

questions.prompt: What evidence establishes a library's responsibility and migration status? Explain the lesson's ZDRxCore naming mismatch and promise-to-async boundary.
questions.scenario: A guide calls a module RxSwift-based, but the lesson traces a ReactiveKit dependency and re-export. PromiseKit bridges coexist with preferred Swift Concurrency guidance.
questions.androidBridge: Android dependencyInsight and RxJava-to-coroutines migrations suggest graph and consumer audits. A Swift module name does not establish its implementation, and converting a promise to async does not automatically inherit Kotlin structured cancellation semantics.
rubric: Uses active manifests, consumer edges, pins, and source imports together.
Distinguishes remote, local, system, vendored, and tooling dependencies.
Interprets the lesson's ReactiveKit evidence over a misleading module name.
Treats preferred concurrency direction as distinct from completed migration.
Checks bridge cancellation, failures, buffering, and completion ownership.
questions.answerHTML:
Start with the graph route being evaluated: dependency manifest, consumer target edges, relevant resolution, and source membership/imports. A pin can be transitive or test-only, and a build plugin is not automatically a runtime SDK. Separate transport, generated models, domain operations, UI, identity, and observability responsibilities instead of listing names without consumers.

The lesson's audit traces ZDRxCore to ReactiveKit despite RxSwift wording in a guide. That concrete dependency and re-export evidence should govern the explanation.
